areas.name: Map and terrain
areas.evidence: One hand-drawn 24x16 map; 6 of 14 land terrains and 7 of 13 resources exist. The map cannot be scrolled with the wheel, keys or touch, and has no zoom. Forts are never drawn.

areas.name: Workers and jobs
areas.evidence: The 7 start civilians work and their jobs, costs and durations match the rules. Several clicks fail silently or spend $1,000 to $5,000 with no price shown. Levels 2 and 3 need no technology.

areas.name: Transport
areas.evidence: Rail, depots, ports and 15 freight cars work. The sliders limit nothing, and the depot network cannot be seen. River ports and blockades are not modelled.

areas.name: Industry and capital
areas.evidence: 7 of 8 production buildings work end to end (armaments to Regulars in 2 turns, paper to a trained worker). Gaps: the dialog is cut off at 1280x720, and the refinery, fuel and power plant are unreachable.

areas.name: Market and trade
areas.evidence: Bids, offers, favourite partner and subsidies work. Trade is capped at 4 units a turn, 10 of 17 Board rows can never trade, prices are a random walk, and orders are forgotten each turn.

areas.name: Diplomacy
areas.evidence: Consulate, embassy, pact, grants, war and peace work. An alliance is only a flag, nothing explains what an overture does, and Join the Empire is not built.

areas.name: Armies and war
areas.evidence: Era-1 land war works against Arvelia: Armoury, marches, battles, conquest. Three of four minors cannot be reached. Horses are finite, and a $100 shortfall disbands the whole army.

areas.name: Council of Governors
areas.evidence: Meetings on turns 10, 20, 30 and 40 run, but the vote can never be won peacefully (best 8 of the 9 votes needed) and the labels contradict the counts.

areas.name: Computer nations
areas.evidence: The computer runs an economy and trades about 1 unit a turn. It starts a war in a third of games, never recruits workers, never attacks you and never defends.

areas.name: Save and load
areas.evidence: No save, no load, no warning before you lose the game by reloading or closing the tab.

areas.name: Technology
areas.evidence: 5 flags exist, 3 of them given free. Nothing can be bought; the Technology button is disabled. The original has 28 technologies.

areas.name: University
areas.evidence: No University and no Developer: a nation has exactly 7 civilians for the whole game.

areas.name: Ships and navy
areas.evidence: No Shipyard, no merchant ships (4 cargo holds for the whole game), no navy, no sea transport.

areas.name: World variety
areas.evidence: One map, 2 Great Powers, 4 minor nations of 1 province each; no difficulty, scenarios or options; the game is always 40 turns.

areas.name: UI and small screens
areas.evidence: All 7 main dialogs fit at 5 desktop sizes and the art pack is applied everywhere. The side panel hides the tile info, a double click ends two turns, and phone width breaks.

areas.name: New-player guidance
areas.evidence: No goal text, no tutorial, no hint after an idle first turn; nothing tells a new player to start with the Capital.

themes.title: No save or load
themes.plain: Reloading the page, going back or closing the tab destroys the game, with no warning.

worst.text: Reloading the page throws the whole game away.
Going back or closing the tab does the same, and nothing warns you first.
There is no way to save a game at all, so a 40-turn game cannot be paused.

themes.title: Map movement
themes.plain: The map is hard to move around and hard to read.

worst.text: The map cannot be scrolled with the mouse wheel, trackpad, touch or keyboard; only by holding the pointer at the window edge.
Edge scrolling also fires over the HUD buttons, so reaching Advance Turn drags the map away.
No zoom, and at 1920x1080 the small map fills the top-left quarter of the screen.

themes.title: Tile panel, news and refusals out of sight
themes.plain: What you need after a click is below the visible part of the side panel.

worst.text: After you click a tile, its panel is below the fold of the side pane; on small windows it is not visible at all.
A refused order (a prospector sent onto the sea) shows its reason only in that hidden part.
The news box shows 3 of about 19 lines and names places by internal tile ids such as "5-2" that the map does not show.

themes.title: Click and order bugs, hidden costs
themes.plain: Some clicks do something other than what the cursor promises, and some spend a lot of money without asking.

worst.text: One click on the tile panel builds a $5,000 fort with no price and no question, and the finished fort is not drawn anywhere.
An engineer cannot lay the last rail section into the capital: the click silently becomes a plain move and the turn is lost.
The tile panel offers buttons that always fail (Develop farmer on a coal hill, Construct Port inland), and the refusal gives no reason.

themes.title: Transport sliders and depot network
themes.plain: The transport sliders look like controls but limit nothing.

worst.text: Set every slider to 0 and the popup still says "Remaining 15": spare capacity is filled automatically and everything ships.
You cannot see which tiles a depot collects, how much, or whether a line is connected.
Goods shipped this turn arrive after production, so a factory uses them one turn later; nothing says so.

themes.title: Money honesty
themes.plain: The game shows money figures that are not what happens next.

worst.text: A subsidy is shown as "free" but silently cuts all income from that minor, down to $0 at 100%.
The upkeep warning says you have enough cash, then End Turn disbands regiments because a subsidised bid costs more than its reserve.
A $100 shortfall disbands the whole army, and the warning does not say so.

themes.title: War and diplomacy honesty
themes.plain: War and diplomacy screens offer things that cannot happen or explain too little.

worst.text: The game lets you declare war on an island minor that can never be attacked, with no warning.
The computer asks for peace every 3 turns from the first turn of war, before any battle, and its offer can stack on the Battle and Council screens.
The "1st nominee" labels and the news line contradict the vote counts.

themes.title: Robustness and small screens
themes.plain: Fast clicking and small windows break things.

worst.text: A double click on Advance Turn ends two turns; five quick clicks end five, even with no orders given.
At phone width (390x844) the Capital, Diplomacy and Board of Trade dialogs break and the map cannot be used.
At 200 percent browser zoom the HUD shows only its title; turn, date, cash and score sit in a 58 px scroll window.

themes.title: New-player guidance
themes.plain: A new player is told nothing about what to do.

worst.text: No goal text, no tutorial, no first-step prompt; the "n" shortcut is hidden.
The tray of civilians holds unlabelled 24 px figures, and ending the first turn idle says nothing.
There is nothing to sell until turn 3, and the Board of Trade does not say what to do meanwhile.

themes.title: Documents and progress page told the wrong story
themes.plain: The progress page and parts of the docs said "done" where the game was not.

worst.text: "Everything done" was true only for a compact scope: 11 rule topics of the original game had no milestone at all.
The progress data contradicted itself: M4 "done 100%" with both tasks unchecked, M11 "in review" and "done" at once.
Two requirements marked "tested" contradict each other (orders take effect at End Turn versus when submitted), and "tested" means less than a reader expects.

themes.title: Computer nations do not play
themes.plain: The computer nations barely play: they rarely start a war, never recruit, and never fight back.

worst.text: The computer starts a war in only a third of games; in the rest it stalls with up to $15,000 idle.
When invaded it never recruits and loses 3 of its 4 provinces in 3 turns.
It never attacks you and never defends, so a conquest win on turn 13 needs only 9 regiments.

themes.title: A game that cannot end well
themes.plain: Games cannot end by diplomacy, and the final ranking and score reward the wrong things.

worst.text: A Council vote can never be won peacefully: the best possible is 8 votes of the 9 needed, and no game ended by Council in 376 meetings.
The final ranking ignores provinces: a nation with 1 of 12 provinces can rank first.
Conquering Arvelia on turn 2 adds 109 points (45% of the start score) with no development work; trade profit of $24,621 earned only 246.

themes.title: People and ships
themes.plain: The player never gets more civilians, ships or horses than at the start.

worst.text: No University: you have exactly the 7 starting civilians for the whole game.
Trade is capped at 4 units a turn for the whole game: no Shipyard, the cargo holds never grow.
Horses have no source: the 4 start horses cap Hussars, Cuirassiers and Light Artillery at 4 units in total, for the computer too.
No technology tree: the original has 28 technologies; the game has 5 flags, 3 of them given free, and nothing can be bought.
Development levels 2 and 3 and the Rancher, Forester and Driller need no technology: the whole ladder is open on turn 1.
The Oil Refinery, Fuel and Power Plant can never be reached, and the Technology button is permanently disabled.

themes.title: Sea war and reach
themes.plain: Merchant ships carry trade. Armies still have no way to reach the three island minors.

worst.text: Three of the four minor nations (Sundmark, Lorran, Pellis) can never be attacked or taken: no ships, no landing.
No navy: fleets are empty lists and the interceptions phase is an unfinished TODO.
Armies move one province a turn with no rail or sea transport, so the start army needs 2 turns to reach Arvelia.

themes.title: World variety and depth
themes.plain: One small hand-drawn world, and many rules of the original are left out.

worst.text: Only 6 of 14 land terrains and 7 of 13 resources exist: no wool, fish, horses, oil, gold, gems, mountains, swamp, desert, tundra or rivers.
One hand-drawn map for every game: no random or key-word maps, no choice of nations, no difficulty.
No Developer, overseas profit or Join the Empire: minor nations are only trading partners, and conquest is the only way to a colony.

decisions.title: Should the game save itself automatically, in this browser only?
decisions.context: Today reloading, going back or closing the tab destroys a 40-turn game with no warning (UIV-01).

options.label: Default: one autosave slot in the browser
options.means: Saved after every turn and every batch of orders. Versioned: a save from an older game version is refused with a message. The start screen offers Continue; New game asks to confirm; the leave-page warning appears only when there is unsaved work.

options.label: Several slots
options.means: You can keep a save before a risky war. More screens to build and test.

options.label: Save to a file you download
options.means: Works across browsers and devices, but needs file handling and is more work.

decisions.suggestion: The default. It fixes the lost-game problem tonight with the least code.
decisions.objection: One slot means a bad late move cannot be undone by loading an earlier turn, and clearing the browser's site data deletes the game.
decisions.ruling: Nathan, 2026-11-16 ("Q79 your suggestion, Q80, Q81, Q82, Q83 your suggestion"): the default below, built in M12 (FR-357 to FR-363).

decisions.title: Should a transport slider you set be a hard limit?
decisions.context: Today every slider limits nothing: set all to 0 and "Remaining 15" still ships everything (ECONOMY-01).

options.label: Default: a slider you set is a hard cap
options.means: An untouched slider means automatic, as today. Spare capacity is not given to a commodity whose slider you set.

options.label: Sliders are only priorities
options.means: Capacity is always used; a slider decides who goes first. The control stays, but "0" does not stop shipping.

decisions.suggestion: The default. A control that does what it says is the point of the fix.
decisions.objection: A forgotten low slider can starve a factory without any message.
decisions.ruling: Nathan, 2026-11-16 ("Q79 your suggestion, Q80, Q81, Q82, Q83 your suggestion"): the default below, built in M12 (FR-389, FR-390).

decisions.title: Where should refusals and errors be shown?
decisions.context: Today the reason for a refused order shows only in the lower part of the side panel, which is below the fold (UIV-04, UIV-05).

options.label: Default: a message on the map, and the tile panel moves to the top of the side pane
options.means: You see the reason where you clicked. The news box moves lower.

options.label: Keep the reason in the news box only
options.means: No layout change, but the reason stays easy to miss.

decisions.suggestion: The default.
decisions.objection: A message strip on the map can cover tiles at the map edge, and a taller tile panel pushes the news further down.
decisions.ruling: Nathan, 2026-11-16 ("Q79 your suggestion, Q80, Q81, Q82, Q83 your suggestion"): the default below, built in M12 (FR-371, FR-373).

decisions.title: Should a costly order ask once before it spends?
decisions.context: Today one click can spend $1,000 to $5,000 on a level 2 or 3 job or a fort with no price shown (ECONOMY-04, ECONOMY-10).

options.label: Default: orders of $1,000 or more, and every fort, show the price and ask once
options.means: The cancel text also says what money comes back.

options.label: Show the price but never ask
options.means: Faster play; a mis-click still spends the money.

options.label: Ask for every order
options.means: Safest, but slow for a 40-turn game.

decisions.suggestion: The default.
decisions.objection: More clicks for an experienced player on every big order.
decisions.ruling: Nathan, 2026-11-16 ("Q79 your suggestion, Q80, Q81, Q82, Q83 your suggestion"): the default below, built in M12 (FR-383, FR-386, FR-422).

decisions.title: Should war on a minor with no land border be blocked until ships exist?
decisions.context: Today the game offers war on Sundmark, Lorran and Pellis, which can never be attacked (ARMY-WAR-05, FR-TRUTH-01).

options.label: Default: the button is disabled with the reason "no land route (needs ships)" until M17
options.means: You cannot start a war that has no way to be fought.

options.label: Allow the declaration
options.means: You could still cut relations by war (a -40 relation step) but could never attack.

decisions.suggestion: The default.
decisions.objection: It also removes the option to declare such a war only to change relations.
decisions.ruling: Nathan, 2026-11-16 ("Q79 your suggestion, Q80, Q81, Q82, Q83 your suggestion"): the default below, built in M12 (FR-406, FR-407).

decisions.title: Centre and zoom the map?
decisions.context: Today the map has no zoom, and on a large screen the small map sits in the top-left corner: at 1920x1080 it fills about a quarter of the screen and the rest is empty sea (UIV-10).

options.label: Default: centre only when there is room, and zoom in three steps
options.means: The map is centred on an axis only when more than 64 px are spare, so 1280x720 looks as it does today. Zoom steps are 100%, 150% and 200%.

options.label: Always centre; free zoom with the wheel
options.means: Looks the same on every screen and zooms smoothly, but the 1280x720 layout moves and every map layer must follow a continuous scale.

decisions.suggestion: The default. It fixes the large-screen look without moving the screens that are already checked.
decisions.objection: Zoom touches every map layer (ground, rail, borders, arrows, cursors); if it cannot keep the 100% checks green inside the lane, the row parks as blocked rather than shipping half done.

decisions.title: How does the keyboard reach the map?
decisions.context: Today the map tiles cannot be reached with the keyboard, so a keyboard-only player cannot select a tile or give any map order (UIV-11).

options.label: Default: the map is one Tab stop
options.means: Tab reaches the map once, the arrow keys move between tiles, and Enter acts on the focused tile.

options.label: Every tile is a Tab stop
options.means: Simple to build, but 384 Tab stops must be crossed before the keyboard reaches the rest of the page.

decisions.suggestion: The default. 384 Tab stops would make every other control hard to reach.
decisions.objection: Screen readers then hear only the focused tile, not the whole map.

decisions.title: Keep the plain-move fallback of a refused job?
decisions.context: Today a rail click onto a tile that already has a job, and the last rail section into the capital, silently become a plain move: no rail, no message, and the civilian's turn is lost (ECONOMY-24, ECONOMY-02).

options.label: Default: keep the fallback and say so
options.means: A refused job still moves the civilian (FR-023). The status line says that the job was refused and why, and Cancel undoes the move.

options.label: No fallback
options.means: A refused job moves nothing and shows the reason. A click that was meant as a move needs a second click.

decisions.suggestion: The default. It keeps what players already rely on and removes the silence.
decisions.objection: A player who misses the line still loses the civilian's turn.

decisions.title: Clicking another civilian: select it or move onto it?
decisions.context: Today clicking another civilian while one is selected moves the selected one next to it instead of switching the selection, and there is no other way to deselect (ECONOMY-08).

options.label: Default: select it
options.means: The click switches the selection. A move onto that tile is a click on the tile beside the button.

options.label: Keep "move here" and switch with a modifier key
options.means: Moving onto a crowded tile stays one click; switching the selection needs a key held down.

decisions.suggestion: The default. A click on a figure should select it.
decisions.objection: Moving onto a crowded tile needs a more careful click.

decisions.title: Draw forts on the map?
decisions.context: Today forts are never drawn on the map (not even the one the Engineer builds for $5,000), only level 1 exists, and the Attack screen is the only place that shows one (ARMY-WAR-10, ECONOMY-04). This replaces the default "no" of card Q74.

options.label: Default: draw a fort mark
options.means: A 16 px fort mark on every tile with a fort, with "Fort level 1" in its title and in Tile Info.

options.label: Tile Info only
options.means: The map stays as crowded as today; a fort is visible only after you click the tile.

decisions.suggestion: The default. A $5,000 building should be visible.
decisions.objection: One more mark on the crowded capital tiles.

decisions.title: Trade orders are forgotten every turn: what helps?
decisions.context: Today trade bids and offers are cleared every turn, while production orders in the same Capital dialog persist (MKT-04, RULES-GAP-12). Card Q15 was answered on 2026-11-09 with one-turn trade orders and a repeat button "if play feels tedious"; the audit found it tedious: up to four clicks a turn for 40 turns.

options.label: Default: a repeat button on the Board of Trade
options.means: Built from the order log, with no engine change, so no test baseline moves. One click repeats last turn's orders.

options.label: Standing orders as in Imperialism 1997
options.means: Orders stay until you change them (rules 06 section 2). An engine change that would replace the answer to Q15 (NR-018).

decisions.suggestion: The default. It removes most of the clicks without touching the engine.
decisions.objection: It is still one click a turn, and the 1997 game kept orders by itself.

decisions.title: How does a tie between Great Powers for a minor's favour break?
decisions.context: Today the favourite partner of a minor flips every turn when two Great Powers have equal relations, against the fixed order in the rules (MKT-11).

options.label: Default: an order fixed per minor for the whole game
options.means: Derived from the seed, so the favourite never flips by turn parity and neither nation is favoured overall.

options.label: The rules' fixed Great Power order
options.means: Nation 1 always comes first. Matches the 1997 rule, but goes against architecture decision 5 and favours one nation in every game.

decisions.suggestion: The default.
decisions.objection: One nation may hold the tie with a given minor for the whole game by luck of the seed.

decisions.title: Should the score stop punishing investment?
decisions.context: Today the score formula punishes investment: ordering a job lowers the score at once, and level 3 development costs 50 points for +10 (ECONOMY-23).

options.label: Default: count what you paid for
options.means: Unfinished paid jobs count at their price / 100, and level 3 is worth 50 points (its $5,000).

options.label: Keep FR-067 and only explain it
options.means: The score stays as it is and the game says why it drops (FR-404).

decisions.suggestion: The default. A score that falls when you invest teaches the wrong play.
decisions.objection: It changes every score and the scripted player's numbers, and NR-018 had kept the score weights for v1.

decisions.title: When does the computer ask for peace?
decisions.context: Today Valdoria asks for peace every 3 turns from the first turn of war, before any battle, and the offer, the Battle screen and the Council dialog can stack at turn start (ARMY-WAR-17, diplomacy-council-16).

options.label: Default: only after a loss
options.means: The computer offers peace only after it lost a province or a battle in this war, and not again for 6 turns after a refusal. Its answers to the player's offers stay (FR-174).

options.label: Keep "weaker than the enemy" and slow the offers down
options.means: The trigger stays as it is; the offers come less often.

decisions.suggestion: The default.
decisions.objection: A computer that is badly outnumbered but not yet beaten never offers peace.

decisions.title: What does closing Accept Offer do?
decisions.context: Today closing an Accept Offer with the x cannot be undone: the offer is gone from every screen for the turn. The dialog and the alliance flow cannot happen in normal play and have no browser test (diplomacy-council-19, FR-TRUTH-10).

options.label: Default: the x hides the dialog
options.means: The offer stays answerable in Diplomacy until End Turn, then it is refused.

options.label: The x refuses at once
options.means: After asking "Refuse this offer?". Final, but no forgotten offers.

decisions.suggestion: The default.
decisions.objection: An offer can be forgotten in Diplomacy and refused by default.

decisions.title: Council nominees: by standing or by votes?
decisions.context: Today "1st nominee / 2nd nominee" and the news line contradict the vote counts (diplomacy-council-08).

options.label: Default: the screen keeps the standing order and says so
options.means: The screen keeps FR-313's standing order and names it; the news line orders by votes.

options.label: Order both by votes
options.means: One order everywhere, but the standing order of FR-313 is no longer shown.

decisions.suggestion: The default.
decisions.objection: The screen and the news then list the nominees in different orders (as card Q58 already notes).

decisions.title: Guard Advance Turn how?
decisions.context: Today Advance Turn has no guard: a double click ends two turns and five quick clicks end five, even with all civilians idle and no orders given (UIV-20). A new player is also not told that civilians are idle (UIV-21).

options.label: Default: a short lock and an information line
options.means: A 600 ms lock after each End Turn and a "civilians without orders" line, but no question.

options.label: Ask first
options.means: A question such as "End the turn with 7 civilians idle?" before every such End Turn.

decisions.suggestion: The default.
decisions.objection: Ending a turn with idle civilians on purpose is common late in a game, so a question would nag; the line only informs.

decisions.title: Are phones supported?
decisions.context: Today at phone width (390x844) the Capital, Diplomacy and Board of Trade dialogs break and the map cannot be used; on the Board the Bid and Offer columns sit 623 px off to the side (UIV-12, MKT-15).

options.label: Default: no, but nothing breaks
options.means: Below 700 px a line says the game is made for 1024 px and wider, the map pans by touch, and the Capital, Board of Trade and Diplomacy dialogs stay readable and closable.

options.label: A full phone layout
options.means: For example the HUD as a bottom sheet. A large piece of work that is its own milestone.

decisions.suggestion: The default.
decisions.objection: The page's viewport tag invites phones.

decisions.title: Make the Capital dialog fit 1280x720, or show that it scrolls?
decisions.context: Today the Capital dialog is cut off at 1280x720 and 1366x768: the Clothing factory card and the Transport footer need an inner scroll that is easy to miss (ECONOMY-17, UIV-14).

options.label: Default: show that it scrolls
options.means: An always-visible scrollbar and a fade on a column that does not fit.

options.label: A denser layout that fits 1280x720
options.means: Nothing is cut off, but the fits of FR-352 are already tight and every dialog row gets smaller.

decisions.suggestion: The default.
decisions.objection: The Clothing factory card still starts below the fold.

decisions.title: When does "How to play" open?
decisions.context: Today a new player gets no hint what to do: no goal text, no tutorial, no first-step prompt, a hidden "n" shortcut, and no guidance for the first turns of trade (ECONOMY-11, UIV-21, MKT-12).

options.label: Default: on the first new game in this browser
options.means: It also opens from About at any time.

options.label: On every new game, or a tutorial
options.means: Every new game shows it; or a tutorial walks through turn 1, which is more to build and test.

decisions.suggestion: The default.
decisions.objection: A second player on the same browser never sees it unless they open About.

decisions.title: A small upkeep shortfall disbands the whole army: change the rule?
decisions.context: Today a $100 upkeep shortfall disbands the whole army, the warning does not say so, and its wording contradicts itself ("$50 is due ... and $16 will be left") (ECONOMY-21, ARMY-WAR-13, MKT-07).

options.label: Default: no rule change in M12
options.means: The warning says exactly how many regiments go. Credit and debt (rules 06 section 6, Nation.creditLimit) come with M18.

options.label: Pay what the treasury holds
options.means: Disband only the regiments the rest cannot pay. A rule change in the engine.

decisions.suggestion: The default. M12 adds no game system; the wording fix is enough for now.
decisions.objection: The rule still wipes out an army for a $100 gap.

decisions.title: NR-016 says orders wait for End Turn; FR-021 says they apply at once. Which holds?
decisions.context: Today two requirements marked "tested" contradict each other (FR-TRUTH-09). In the code, only freight cars wait for End Turn; every other order applies when it is given.

options.label: Default: the code's behaviour (FR-021)
options.means: Orders apply when given, with a full same-turn cancel. The status of NR-016 says so; queued orders are not planned.

options.label: Build queued orders
options.means: Orders wait for End Turn as NR-016 says. A large engine change, later.

decisions.suggestion: The default. It matches what players see and what the tests check.
decisions.objection: NR-016 was Nathan's own decision (Q9).

decisions.title: The v1 "World market" dialog cannot be reached in the app: show it or document it?
decisions.context: Today Open Market always opens the Board of Trade, so the v1 World market dialog (FR-073, FR-074, FR-078) cannot be reached in the app (MKT-05).

options.label: Default: document it as a test-only fixture
options.means: The three rows say that they are tested in unit tests on the two-islands world and not reachable in the app.

options.label: A New game option for the v1 world
options.means: Players can open it; more screens to keep working.

decisions.suggestion: The default.
decisions.objection: FR-073, FR-074 and FR-078 describe a screen no player can see.

decisions.title: Hide the Debug box?
decisions.context: Today a "Debug" box with the tile id and the game seed is shown to every player in the HUD (ECONOMY-18, UIV-07).

options.label: Default: shown only with ?debug in the URL
options.means: Players do not see it; anyone who adds ?debug to the address does.

options.label: Remove it
options.means: Gone for everyone, including you; the seed is then harder to read out.

decisions.suggestion: Not taken: Nathan ruled the other way (see Ruled).
decisions.ruling: Nathan, 2026-11-16: "keep the debug". The bug-report details stay and show without ?debug, in a closed group "Details for bug reports" in the right pane (FR-476, built in M12b). This replaces the default above and ends FR-377's ?debug rule once M12b is built.

decisions.title: A baseline moves: keep the old behaviour or re-record the number?
decisions.context: Several M12 changes move numbers that tests pin for the scripted player: transport sliders (FR-389), the favourite partner (FR-401) and the score (FR-403). This card has no finding of its own; the ids are the findings behind those three changes (FR-405). Measured at the M12 integration: FR-403 and the 1.5 margin conflict. The frozen M4 player's level-3 tiles gain 40 points each, the scripted player builds none, and the margin at turn 15 falls to 1.39 to 1.46 (FR-125 red, not loosened). Choose: an AI task for the scripted player's early economy, a lower turn-15 margin, or a smaller level-3 value. Review round 2 (2026-11-16): changing the scripted player's cash reserve ($1,500 to $6,000) leaves the lowest turn-15 ratio at 1.35 to 1.42, so the AI task is a work item of its own, not a constant. Update 2026-11-16: the AI task was done (M12 strategy C, FR-454 to FR-458): the scripted player holds the 1.5 margin on seeds 1 to 4 (lowest 1.50, seed 3 at turn 25), so FR-125 is green again; the baselines that moved were re-recorded with their reasons (Q105 to Q107).

options.label: Default: re-record the number with its reason
options.means: Never loosen a check; keep NR-023's margin.

options.label: Keep the scripted player's old behaviour
options.means: Special cases in the engine so that old numbers stay true.

decisions.suggestion: The default. The reason is written next to the number.
decisions.objection: Re-recorded baselines stop proving that nothing else changed.

decisions.title: Cap offers at the buyers' demand in the engine or on the Board only?
decisions.context: Today the Board of Trade lets you offer more units than the minor buyers take; the surplus wastes a cargo hold (ECONOMY-20).

options.label: Default: the Board only
options.means: The Board stops you at the demand. The engine still accepts a larger offer and returns the surplus.

options.label: The engine refuses it
options.means: The engine returns "limit-reached" for a larger offer, for every player including the scripted one.

decisions.suggestion: The default.
decisions.objection: A scripted or future LLM player can still waste a hold.

decisions.title: Keep the paper rule that changed three v1 turn-1 test cases, or turn it off on the two-islands world?
decisions.context: What happened: FR-159 (decision 1) says the v1 two-islands tests keep their numbers. The new rule FR-455 (the computer makes no paper for training while its workers can already handle everything its depots bring in) changes what it makes on turn 1, so three turn-1 test cases were re-recorded: in twoNations.test.ts the trade orders of newGame(11) (nation 1 now buys steel 2, lumber 1, steel 3 and sells timber 1; before: lumber 1, steel 1, lumber 2, steel 2 and timber 1) and the goods-first test (after the furniture it now bids for steel 2; before: lumber 1 and steel 1), and in scriptedScore.test.ts the FR-129 plan (lumber 2 and no paper; before: paper 2). Without FR-455 the computer falls below the 1.5 margin at turn 15 (1.41 to 1.48, FR-125 red). The default below is in the code now; nothing waits on it.

options.label: Default: keep FR-455 everywhere
options.means: The three turn-1 test cases stay re-recorded and FR-159 gets a new row that accepts them. The computer keeps the 1.5 margin on every seed and checkpoint (lowest 1.60, seed 3 turn 25, since FR-460).

options.label: Turn FR-455 off for the v1 two-islands world
options.means: The three turn-1 test cases pass with their old numbers again, but the margin test, which runs on two-islands, fails at turn 15 (1.41 to 1.48) and needs another fix or an answer to Q103.

decisions.suggestion: The default: FR-455 is what makes the margin hold, and the three test cases that moved pin turn-1 orders, not a rule a player relies on.
decisions.objection: FR-159 was decision 1: the v1 tests were meant to prove that v1 play did not change, and three of their cases no longer do.

decisions.title: The rail check at turns 15, 25 and 40 sees a rail still being laid: keep it strict, or let it skip the end of a rail going to a built depot?
decisions.context: What happened: FR-125's check "no dead end at any checkpoint" (a rail end that is not a depot, NR-022) passes on seeds 1 to 4, but by timing. On seeds 3 and 4 the depot 20-2 gets its two rail sections on turns 24 and 25, so the open end 19,2 is gone at the turn-25 checkpoint by one turn. Before FR-459 the sections came on turns 25 and 28 and the check was red; FR-459 removed the block (a forester working on 20-2), but that alone would have laid them on turns 25 and 26, still red; the check cleared because the rail also came one turn earlier. A rail being laid always has an open end for a turn or more: on the continent (start army, its default market) every seed 1 to 16 has one at 15,8 at turn 15, where no test looks. So any later AI change that moves the rail by one turn can turn the check red with nothing wrong. The strategy C gate listed this decision with no card; this is that card. FR-459 and FR-460 removed the two things that kept the engineer from laying a section (a job on the tile, a training that spent his cash). The default below is how the test is now; nothing waits on it.

options.label: Default: keep the check strict
options.means: Nothing changes. The check is green on seeds 1 to 4 today. A later AI change that shifts a depot's rail by one turn can make it red with no fault in the rail, and the next agent has to show it is timing, as this review did.

options.label: Let the check skip the open end of a rail going to a built depot
options.means: A new FR row: an open end on the shortest path to a built depot that is not joined yet is not a dead end. The check stops depending on timing and still catches rail that leads to no depot. It no longer proves the rail is finished at the checkpoint (FR-125's other check, a depot joined, still holds).

decisions.suggestion: The second option: NR-022 is about rail that joins nothing, and a rail on its way to a built depot is not that. The test's own comment already says a path being laid has an open end for a few turns.
decisions.objection: It changes a test's check (FR-405: no check is loosened to hide a change, so only Nathan can choose it), and a real dead end that happens to lie on the way to a built depot would then pass.

decisions.title: Should a nation with an army also keep its civilians' cash when it trains workers?
decisions.context: What happened: the computer plans its economy before its civilians, so training could spend the cash the engineer needed for his next rail section. FR-460 makes a nation without an army keep its reserve (FR-454: $100 a developer plus a depot or a rail section) when it trains; on two-islands seeds 7 and 15 a depot no longer joins a turn late. A nation with an army still trains as before. Measured on the continent (world market, start army): on seed 7, turn 15 four trainings to expert left $264, and the engineer's $100 section was dropped because it would take the treasury under the army's upkeep floor of $200 (FR-213). Keeping a reserve there too costs score: the whole reserve ($2,500) lowered FR-260's start-army scores on seeds 2, 3 and 4 (1546 -> 1521, 1548 -> 1531, 1685 -> 1630); only the civilians' share plus the upkeep lowered seed 2 (1546 -> 1495). The default below is in the code now; nothing waits on it.

options.label: Default: a nation with an army trains as before
options.means: FR-260's start-army scores stay as they are (1507, 1546, 1548, 1685). Its engineer can still wait a turn for a section when training spends the cash.

options.label: Every nation keeps its civilians' cash when it trains
options.means: The engineer is never kept from a section by training. FR-260's start-army scores drop by up to 55 points and are re-recorded; with the whole reserve the FR-247 trade baseline moves too.

decisions.suggestion: The default: the score loss is measured, the engineer was kept from a section once in eight games (seed 7, turn 15), and the armed nation's campaign needs its trained workers (FR-458).
decisions.objection: The same fault FR-460 fixes for a nation without an army stays for a nation with one.

decisions.title: Should the top bar have Army and Council buttons?
decisions.context: The original game has an army panel on the map screen. Here no standing screen exists behind such buttons: the Army screen needs a province (it opens from the map) and the Council screen only replays a meeting from the news. Council information sits in the turn block and the Nation group.

options.label: Default: not now
options.means: The bar holds the six dialog buttons, Center, New game, About and Advance Turn. No new behaviour.

options.label: Army and Council buttons
options.means: "Army" opens the Army screen for the capital's province; "Council" opens the last meeting (disabled before turn 10). Small, but new behaviour that needs its own rows.

decisions.suggestion: Not now, no Army or Council button.
decisions.objection: The original has an army panel on the map screen, so players of the first game may look for it.

decisions.title: New game and About as two buttons or a Game menu, and is a Save button needed?
decisions.context: The top bar needs a place for New game and About. Autosave runs on every order (FR-357, FR-358) and the "Not saved" alert covers the failure case.

options.label: Default: two plain buttons, no Save button
options.means: Names stay for the e2e suite and no extra click.

options.label: A "Game" menu with New game, About and Save
options.means: Fewer buttons in the bar; hides the names from the e2e suite and adds a click.

decisions.suggestion: Two plain buttons and no Save button.
decisions.objection: New game sits near Advance Turn and could be clicked by mistake. The FR-109 question already guards it.

decisions.title: Should the right pane show a Warehouse summary group?
decisions.context: Open Warehouse is one click away in the top bar. A group with food, coal and iron would save that click while placing civilians.

options.label: Default: no group
options.means: One copy of the stock list, in the Warehouse dialog.

options.label: A "Warehouse summary" group
options.means: Food, coal and iron in the pane; a second copy of the stock list to keep in step.

decisions.suggestion: No group now.
decisions.objection: Seeing coal and grain while placing civilians saves a dialog round trip. It could come later as one line (food, coal, iron).

decisions.title: Should the war lines stay always in sight, or move into the Nation group?
decisions.context: A war is rare and must not be missed. The alerts block under Tile Info costs 16 px per war.

options.label: Default: always in sight
options.means: In the alerts under Tile Info, with the other warnings.

options.label: Inside the Nation group
options.means: A calmer pane; the war line is hidden until the group is opened.

decisions.suggestion: Always in sight.
decisions.objection: The brief put the war lines in the Nation group to keep the pane calm.

decisions.title: With no tile selected, should the pane show a placeholder line or nothing?
decisions.context: FR-315 removed the "No tile selected" hint only to save space; the new pane has the room.

options.label: Default: one line
options.means: "No tile selected: click a tile on the map." It tells where Tile Info appears.

options.label: Nothing
options.means: As FR-315 says today.

decisions.suggestion: One line, the placeholder stays.
decisions.objection: One more line of text that says nothing new to a returning player.

decisions.title: Where does Advance Turn sit?
decisions.context: The HUD redesign moves the buttons out of the right pane. The spec suggested the top bar's right end; in the original, End Turn is a bar at the bottom of the right column. The other option was a full-width Advance Turn at the pane's bottom (about 40 px).
decisions.ruling: Nathan, 2026-11-16: "one STATIC end turn is enough, just do not force me to scroll to find it at the bottom". So: exactly one Advance Turn button, always on screen, never scrolled away and never at the bottom of a scrolling pane. It is the top bar's right end (FR-466); FR-467 tests it at 1280x720, 800x600 and 390x844 on turn 1 and with a long news list.

decisions.title: Should the computer go to war with the player?
decisions.context: After Arvelia falls (turn 16 or 17 in every game), the computer has nothing left to do for 23 turns. The rules report that the AI declares war when the military balance is lopsided (rules 10 section 3). Decides FR-488 (War on the other Great Power).

options.label: Option (a)
options.means: Never, as today: an idle player is never threatened.

options.label: Option (b), suggested
options.means: From turn 20, when its field army is twice the defence of our weakest border province, with limited aims (Q115).

options.label: Option (c)
options.means: Like (b), but also earlier and at random, by a "personality".

decisions.suggestion: Option (b).
decisions.objection: A new or idle player loses a province around turn 25 in most games, and many continent pins move. Some testers will call a punished idle player unfair. The FR-495 warning is the answer to that.
decisions.needed: Nathan accepted option (b) for the current 40-turn game on 2026-11-17. NR-035 calls for separate war-start rules for each future difficulty level. See docs/specs/war-and-difficulty-notes.md.

decisions.title: What does the computer want from a war with the player?
decisions.context: Decides FR-489 (One province, then peace).

options.label: Option (a), suggested
options.means: One province, then peace offers every 6 turns.

options.label: Option (b)
options.means: Fight on while the estimate allows, which can take the capital and end the game by conquest.

options.label: Option (c)
options.means: Take everything except the capital province.

decisions.suggestion: Option (a).
decisions.objection: It is predictable, and an expert player can bait it, for example by leaving a province weak on purpose. The Imp1 AI re-declares when it thinks the player took too much.
decisions.needed: Nathan accepted option (a) for M13 on 2026-11-17. The one-province aim and peace offers every six turns are temporary. NR-035 calls for war-stop rules per difficulty level.

decisions.title: Recruit workers: only to replace losses, or also to staff the mills?
decisions.context: NR-028 says the computer recruits to use its capacity. M4.4 measured that this lowers its score by about 6%, and FR-125's thinnest margin is 58.5 points (seed 3, turn 25: 903 against 844.5 needed), so a 6% loss would leave about 4. Decides FR-485 (Migrants keep the workforce), FR-486 (The mills it builds are staffed).

options.label: Option (a)
options.means: FR-485 only: replace the workers its regiments took.

options.label: Option (b), suggested
options.means: (a) plus FR-486, on worlds with provinces only.

options.label: Option (c)
options.means: Both rules on both worlds: FR-125 would most likely fail.

decisions.suggestion: Option (b).
decisions.objection: The scripted player then has two rule sets, and the v1 world no longer shows how the continent AI plays.

decisions.title: How does the computer compete for minors' votes?
decisions.context: Decides FR-490 (Grants before a Council) and FR-542. Before: option (a) was built and gave Valdoria a minor's vote at the turn-30 Council in 0 of 24 idle games (required 18): no embassy, so no grant, in any game. Nobody had answered, so the M13 close round (2026-11-17, branch claude/m13-nations, not merged) built option (b) as FR-542: the embassy from 25 relation points (the start's 30 qualifies), with the minor that has the most points and does not border Valdoria (the campaign's next target), not for the first meeting, kept only above the upkeep reserve, while the recruits and the training keep its $5,000; the pact the turn after; the campaign spares a pact partner. Measured (24 idle games): embassy and pact before the turn-30 meeting in 21, a minor's vote at the turn-30 meeting in 0, at the turn-40 meeting in 18. Not checked by eye in the app.

options.label: Option (a)
options.means: $1,000 grants in the 4 turns before each Council, to the minor where it is between 40 and 49 points and not behind you, with the embassy the grants need from 35 points. Built before the close round: no embassy and no grant in any idle game, 0 of 24 votes.

options.label: Option (b), built
options.means: Also an embassy ($5,000) and a pact (+10 points), as FR-542. A minor at 37 to 48 points with Valdoria at turn 30 (a vote needs 50); 1 vote at turn 40 in 18 of 24 games.

options.label: Option (c)
options.means: None.

decisions.suggestion: Option (b) as built (it was option (a) before the close round; (a) alone gave no embassy and no grant in any game).
decisions.objection: Valdoria pays $5,000 for the embassy and up to $4,000 in grants, about 70 points of its turn-40 score; you may see the pact and the grants as buying votes (Imp1 allows the same); and FR-490's turn-30 promise is still not kept (card Q139).

decisions.title: How do the two Great Powers trade with each other?
decisions.context: Imp1 shows offer sheets from other powers during the turn. Here the computer orders after the player, so the player cannot see its orders of this turn. Decides FR-491 (Last turn's trade orders are public), FR-494 (The Board shows the other Great Power's last turn).

options.label: Option (a), suggested
options.means: Last turn's bids and offers are public; a bid toward the rival is always allowed (refunded if unfilled); an offer is allowed only after the rival bid for that commodity last turn.

options.label: Option (b)
options.means: Imp1's offer sheets: the computer plans before the player each turn (a large change to the turn loop).

options.label: Option (c)
options.means: No trade between Great Powers.

decisions.suggestion: Option (a).
decisions.objection: There is a one-turn lag, and a bid can come back refunded. The Board line says so.

decisions.title: What does the computer recruit, and how low may its cash go when invaded?
decisions.context: Decides FR-482 (Recruit what can be raised), FR-483 (The cash floor under invasion).

options.label: Option (a), suggested
options.means: The two lists in FR-482 and the upkeep reserve as the floor under a threat.

options.label: Option (b)
options.means: Choose by strength per dollar.

options.label: Option (c)
options.means: Keep Regulars only and train fewer workers.

decisions.suggestion: Option (a).
decisions.objection: The lists ignore price, and Cuirassiers use the 4 scarce horses (more horses come in M15).

decisions.title: Should the last Council force every governor to choose?
decisions.context: The rules say yes (rules 01 section 4). Decides FR-501 (Every governor chooses at the last meeting).

options.label: Option (a), suggested
options.means: Yes, by relation points, with no floor.

options.label: Option (b)
options.means: No, as today: most turn-40 meetings end with no winner.

decisions.suggestion: Option (a), default taken for M14. At the final Council each free minor votes by relations with no 50-point floor. War with both nominees forces an abstention.
decisions.objection: Nearly every game gets a "winner" at turn 40 even when both nations are weak, so the score matters less.

decisions.title: How many votes win with only two Great Powers?
decisions.context: Decides FR-503 (Votes needed in a world of two Great Powers).

options.label: Option (a), suggested
options.means: More than half (7 of 12) while fewer than 3 Great Powers exist.

options.label: Option (b)
options.means: Two thirds (9 of 12), as the manual says: a peaceful win stays impossible here.

options.label: Option (c)
options.means: Count each minor as 4 votes (its Imp1 size), so 24 votes and 17 needed.

decisions.suggestion: Option (a), default taken for M14. With fewer than three Great Powers a strict majority elects a nominee (7 of 12). Three or more retain the two-thirds rule.
decisions.objection: It departs from the manual. With Arvelia (from turn 17) and two minors, the computer can win at turn 30.
decisions.needed: Default taken before implementing FR-503 on 2026-11-20. The peaceful election target is 7 of the 12 votes.

decisions.title: Equal votes at the last meeting: who wins?
decisions.context: Decides FR-502 (The last meeting always names a winner).

options.label: Option (a), suggested
options.means: The higher standing.

options.label: Option (b)
options.means: The higher score.

options.label: Option (c)
options.means: Nobody: the game ends on points.

decisions.suggestion: Option (a), default taken for M14. A tied final vote uses standing, then intent order.
decisions.objection: Standing adds 100 per province, so conquest also decides ties.

decisions.title: How should conquered land count in the score?
decisions.context: Decides FR-505 (A conquered province counts when it is collected).

options.label: Option (a), suggested
options.means: Only collected tiles of conquered provinces count.

options.label: Option (b)
options.means: Only collected tiles count anywhere (this also changes home tiles and may move FR-125).

options.label: Option (c)
options.means: No change.

decisions.suggestion: Option (a), default taken for M14. Conquered development counts only where the owner can collect the tile.
decisions.objection: A conqueror who builds a depot gets the points back, and standing still rewards the province itself.

decisions.title: Should a game with no Council name a result?
decisions.context: Decides FR-508 (The end of a game without a Council).

options.label: Option (a), suggested
options.means: "Best score: X".

options.label: Option (b)
options.means: Nothing, as FR-300 says today.

decisions.suggestion: Option (a), default taken for M14. On a world without provinces the turn limit names the nation with the best score.
decisions.objection: How to play calls the best score the goal, but it is the only result on the test world only.

decisions.title: What does each civilian cost at the University?
decisions.context: The rules give 1 expert, 2 paper and $500 to $1,500 (Prospector $500, Miner $1,500 seen). Decides FR-511 (The University).

options.label: Option (a), suggested
options.means: Prospector $500, Miner $1,500, the others $1,000.

decisions.suggestion: Option (a), default taken for M15. Prospector $500, Miner $1,500, the others $1,000.
decisions.objection: A guessed price; an Engineer is the most valuable civilian here and may be too cheap.

decisions.title: How do ships and the computer's fleet start?
decisions.context: Decides FR-514 (Merchant ships), FR-516 (The computer builds ships).

options.label: Option (a), suggested
options.means: The 4 start holds become one Indiaman; the computer builds Indiamen when its holds are full on 3 of 4 turns.

options.label: Option (b)
options.means: The computer starts with 6 to 8 holds, as observed in Imp1.

options.label: Option (c)
options.means: The computer builds no ships.

decisions.suggestion: Option (a), default taken for M15. The 4 start holds become one Indiaman; the computer builds Indiamen when its holds are full on 3 of 4 turns.
decisions.objection: The computer's rule acts only on the continent (to keep FR-125), and lumber spent on ships is lumber not spent on mills.

decisions.title: Where do the Horse Ranch tiles go?
decisions.context: Decides FR-517 (Horses from a ranch).

options.label: Option (a), suggested
options.means: One open-range tile per Great Power within reach of the capital, and one in Arvelia.

options.label: Option (b)
options.means: Only in minors (horses must be bought).

options.label: Option (c)
options.means: None: horses only by trade.

decisions.suggestion: Option (a), default taken for M15. One open-range tile per Great Power within reach of the capital, and one in Arvelia.
decisions.objection: It changes the hand-drawn map, so every continent tile-count pin moves.

decisions.title: Living minors (supply, demand and prices that move): M15 or later?
decisions.context: Living minors have no row yet: M15 leaves them out, and this card asks when they come.

options.label: Option (a), suggested
options.means: A separate M15b after M16.

options.label: Option (b)
options.means: Inside M15 (it would need about 2 more hours).

options.label: Option (c)
options.means: In M18.

decisions.suggestion: Option (a), default taken for M15. A separate M15b after M16.
decisions.objection: Trade stays narrow (3 goods with buyers) for one more milestone.

decisions.title: Should the computer build civilians in M15?
decisions.context: Decides FR-518 (Baselines).

options.label: Option (a), suggested
options.means: No, measure it first (it has one Engineer for all its rail).

options.label: Option (b)
options.means: A second Engineer when it has an expert and $1,000 beyond its reserve.

decisions.suggestion: Option (a), default taken for M15. No, measure it first (it has one Engineer for all its rail).
decisions.objection: The player gets a tool the computer does not use, which is an advantage for the player.

decisions.title: What game length and which technology years should M16 use?
decisions.context: The game ends in Winter 1824. With the rules' real years only 5 technologies can appear (Cotton Gin and the four of 1821 to 1825), and level 2 for farms (Steel and Iron Plows, 1831) would never come. Decides FR-521 (The technology clock).

options.label: Option (a), suggested
options.means: Compress the technology years into the game: 100 years over the turn limit (40 turns: a new set about every 2 turns).

options.label: Option (b)
options.means: The real years, 40 turns: 5 technologies, no level-2 farms.

options.label: Option (c)
options.means: A longer default game (for example 120 turns, 1815 to 1845) with the real years.

decisions.suggestion: Option (a), default taken for M16. Spread 100 technology years across the configured turn limit. TIME_CONFIG.TURN_LIMIT supplies the temporary default of 40.
decisions.objection: The calendar says 1820 while Internal Combustion is for sale, and the late prices ($40,000 to $150,000) are out of reach in 40 turns.
decisions.needed: Default taken for Task 11. Revisit the clock and affordability when the game gains difficulty levels.

decisions.title: Keep NR-015's three free technologies?
decisions.context: Decides FR-520 (Each nation owns its technologies).

options.label: Option (a), suggested
options.means: Keep them (rail on hills, timber levels and the mines' level 3 stay open as today).

options.label: Option (b)
options.means: Remove them: rail on hills waits for Compound Steam Engine (turn 9 under (a) of Q130, $7,000).

decisions.suggestion: Option (a), default taken for M16. Keep Compound Steam Engine, Iron Railroad Bridge and Dynamite alongside the two historical starting technologies.
decisions.objection: Dynamite (an 1871 technology) owned on turn 1 is not the rules.

decisions.title: Do the start civilians need technology?
decisions.context: Decides FR-524 (Civilians need their technology).

options.label: Option (a), suggested
options.means: No, the 7 start civilians stay.

options.label: Option (b)
options.means: Remove the Rancher, Forester and Driller until their technology is bought.

decisions.suggestion: Option (a), default taken for M16. Keep all seven starting civilians. Apply technology prerequisites to recruitment and development.
decisions.objection: A Rancher on turn 1 without Feed Grasses can do nothing until it is bought, which looks like a bug.

decisions.title: Which technology does the computer buy?
decisions.context: Decides FR-527 (The computer buys technology).

options.label: Option (a), suggested
options.means: The cheapest one that unlocks a level it would order.

options.label: Option (b)
options.means: A fixed list from the rules' "recommended early buys" (Iron Railroad Bridge, Square-Set Timbering).

options.label: Option (c)
options.means: None.

decisions.suggestion: The resource-gate branch tried option (a) and is parked. The buyer-only branch proposes FR-547 (Q143), buying for a planned use within three turns. Compare the timing and value of purchases in the original game before choosing a rule for main.
decisions.objection: It ignores ships and military technologies until those milestones exist.

decisions.title: Power Plant, oil and era-2 units: now or later?
decisions.context: The fuel-to-labour rate is not documented, and the map has no oil. Decides FR-525 (What else the technologies unlock now).

options.label: Option (a), suggested
options.means: Later (M17 and M18): the Power Plant, oil and era-2 units wait for the sea war and the world pieces.

options.label: Option (b)
options.means: Now: build the Power Plant and the era-2 units in M16, on a guessed fuel-to-labour rate.

decisions.suggestion: Option (a), default taken for M16. Defer the Power Plant, oil sites, later regiments, forts and warships. Oil Drilling unlocks the Driller and refinery, and Streamlined Hulls unlocks the Clipper.
decisions.objection: Oil Drilling enables training and a refinery, but there are no oil sites to supply it.

decisions.title: What happens to saves made before technologies belong to each nation?
decisions.context: Decides FR-520 (Each nation owns its technologies).

options.label: Option (a), suggested
options.means: Migrate them.

options.label: Option (b)
options.means: Refuse them with FR-362's message.

decisions.suggestion: Option (a), default taken for M16. Migrate version-1 saves by copying purchased shared IDs and legacy oil ownership to each nation.
decisions.objection: One migration function to keep until the next version.

decisions.title: How many votes should a Council win need?
decisions.context: Default: more than two thirds of all votes, 9 of 12, as in the original. With only 2 Great Powers that needs your 4 provinces, all 4 minors and one rival province, so a vote win is rare. Option: more than half (7 of 12) lets diplomacy alone win.
decisions.suggestion: Default in force; reversible.
decisions.audit: The audit found a Council win by votes is impossible today: the best possible is 8 of the 9 votes needed (AISIM-05, FR-TRUTH-02, diplomacy-council-01). With 7 of 12, diplomacy alone could win. M14 needs this answer.

decisions.title: Should taking a Great Power capital give all its provinces to the winner, and taking a minor capital make it a colony?
decisions.context: In 1997 a fallen power falls into anarchy and fights on.
decisions.suggestion: Taken (simpler, ends a 2-power game). Default in force; reversible.
decisions.audit: Related finding: conquest is the cheapest score, +109 points for taking Arvelia on turn 2 (ARMY-WAR-18), and the computer never defends (ARMY-WAR-03). Taking one capital ends the whole game. M14 needs this answer.

decisions.title: Should the computer go to war with the weakest minor from turn 10 when it is twice as strong, never with a Great Power?
decisions.context: It makes the computer compete for minors without threatening the score baselines.
decisions.suggestion: Taken. Default in force; reversible.
decisions.audit: The audit found the computer starts this war in only 19 to 33 percent of games and stalls otherwise (ARMY-WAR-02, AISIM-01). M13 changes this behaviour.

decisions.title: Should the map keep the removed "No tile selected" hint?
decisions.context: The M10 QA round removed the hint under the map because it repeated what an empty side panel already says.
decisions.suggestion: Taken: removed. Default in force; reversible.
decisions.audit: Related: the audit found a new player gets no guidance (ECONOMY-11, UIV-21), so a hint like this may be worth bringing back in M12.

decisions.title: Should the Council news line name the player first, as the Council screen does?
decisions.context: Today the news line names the 1st nominee (most votes) first, while the screen lists the player first.
decisions.suggestion: Taken: news by vote order, screen player first. Default in force; reversible.
decisions.audit: Related: the news line and the nominee labels contradict the vote counts (diplomacy-council-08). M12 touches this text.

decisions.title: Should abstention reasons on the Council screen use relation levels instead of points?
decisions.context: The Council screen says a minor abstains below 50 relation points; the Diplomacy screen shows levels (0 to 8).
decisions.suggestion: Taken: points (exact, matches the rule). Default in force; reversible.
decisions.audit: Related: the player cannot see what decides the minors' votes (diplomacy-council-07). M12 touches this screen.

decisions.title: Borders: nation colours on a pale halo?
decisions.context: The pack's territory line is one brown, so it cannot show which nation owns the land. Alternative: the pack's brown line for all borders plus another ownership cue. The minor's colour (lane 1): the old slate darkened to 3:1 came within 20 of nation 1 under protanopia (FR-154), so the default is #26362c (dark slate green, 6.14:1 on the halo, colour-blind margin to nation 1 only 20.0); alternatives: the hue-kept near black #192127, or relax FR-154's colour-blind distance for the dashed minor line.
decisions.suggestion: Taken: the vector borders stay in nation colours on the pack's halo colour; minor and province colours are darkened to reach 3:1 on the halo (FR-327, FR-329). Default in force; reversible.
decisions.audit: The audit did not flag the colours. The minor's colour-blind margin to nation 1 is thin (20.0). Not part of M12 unless you decide.

decisions.title: A crowded capital: how does it stay recognisable?
decisions.context: (review F2) The civilians' 24 px button covers the middle of any picture that fills the 40 px tile, and a capital holds the start civilians and the army chip, so on turn 1 only the spire showed. Alternatives: move the button and the army chip off the picture (they would then cover the neighbouring tiles), or keep the whole-tile picture covered and add a text cue.
decisions.suggestion: Taken (QA fix round, FR-346): on a capital or town with civilians or a minor's name tag the picture is drawn at 48 px, lifted into the gap between the row above's pictures, with the civilians in the corner and the army chip low; on turn 1 at most 22% of each capital is covered. The first default, 24 px at the top centre (FR-341), still showed only a small dome. Default in force; reversible.
decisions.audit: Related: UIV-22 found the capital picture still mostly covered by the army marker and the civilian stack in the running game.

decisions.title: Transport's picture at 16 px?
decisions.context: (QA fix round) The railyard at 16 px in the HUD and the Transport heading was a brown blob; the depot, the pack's other transport picture, is no clearer at that size. Alternatives: the depot; text only in the HUD.
decisions.suggestion: Taken: keep the railyard and draw it larger: 20 px in the HUD, every full-width action button's icon in the same 20 px box so the labels stay aligned (FR-349, FR-351), and 30 px in the Capital's Transport heading (FR-352). Default in force; reversible.
decisions.audit: Related: UIV-22 found depot and port marks tiny; the railyard size itself was not flagged.

decisions.title: Should the computer recruit workers at all?
decisions.context: Measured in M4.4: with free workers (upper bound) the computer scores 2972 to 5513 against 5925 without, summed over four seeds at turn 40. The best real policy (R2) grows the workforce 7 to 9 and costs about 350 points (6%), margin still 1.57. About 28% of labour is idle; from turn 20 freight cars limit shipping. More cars alone gave +86 (1.4%).
decisions.suggestion: (a) No recruiting in v1 (taken meanwhile); revisit with (c) transport and inputs first when we plan v2 AI work.

decisions.title: Should the v2 world have one land-bridge minor nation and three island minors?
decisions.context: Two land bridges put Valdoria's capital province next to a minor nation (one battle from a capital rush); one bridge keeps both capitals behind other provinces. Options: (a) two bridges; (b) one bridge, three islands; (c) mirrored islands (breaks tile ids). Found in the M5 review: Arvelia's and Lorran's capitals are one step nearer Testland than Valdoria (a small tilt toward the human).
decisions.suggestion: (b) taken: Arvelia bridges the north; Sundmark, Lorran and Pellis are islands (trade only until ships). The tilt is accepted for now; a fix is a 3-tile Lorran centred at 12-1 under a new requirement. Default in force; reversible.

decisions.title: Should each minor nation be one province?
decisions.context: The original has 16 minors of 4 provinces; the 24x16 map fits 4 small ones. (a) one province: a war on a minor is one battle; (b) two provinces each: two battles; (c) a bigger map.
decisions.suggestion: (a) taken; revisit after play. Default in force; reversible.

decisions.title: Should relations move by 10 points a level (+1 a trade, +2 to +8 a grant, +10 a pact, -40 a war)?
decisions.context: No source states the 1997 step sizes; the wiki ladder (about 150 trades to the top) is out of reach in 40 turns.
decisions.suggestion: Taken: about 50 trades or grants from yellow to dark green. Default in force; reversible.

decisions.title: Should both Great Powers start equal with every minor (yellow) and with each other (beige, embassies)?
decisions.context: The original makes minors friendlier to the computer on Normal.
decisions.suggestion: Equal start taken. Default in force; reversible.

decisions.title: Should trading with a minor nation need a consulate?
decisions.context: 1997 rule: anyone can trade; a consulate only makes deals raise relations. The plan rule makes the $500 consulate the first strategic choice.
decisions.suggestion: Consulate needed (plan rule) taken; easy to switch. Default in force; reversible.

decisions.title: Should a minor offer 1 unit per resource tile (at most 6) and buy 2 of each good a turn?
decisions.context: Matches observed 1997 offers (1 to 6 units); demand growth over time is unknown (gap C5).
decisions.suggestion: Taken. Default in force; reversible.

decisions.title: Should the favourite partner rank by relation points plus half the subsidy percent, with deals at the shown board price?
decisions.context: 1997 settles at a clearing price unknown when ordering; the default lets the player know the price in advance.
decisions.suggestion: Taken. Default in force; reversible.

decisions.title: Should the computer accept an alliance at level 7 of 9 and peace when it is losing?
decisions.context: A 1997 guide says AI hatred never stops; the default gives a predictable opponent.
decisions.suggestion: Taken. Default in force; reversible.

decisions.title: Should each Great Power start with 2 Regulars, 1 Artillery, militia and a fort on its capital?
decisions.context: Gives each side enough to take a minor nation early; upkeep $100 a turn like the 1815 ledger.
decisions.suggestion: Taken. Default in force; reversible.

decisions.title: Should regiment costs not seen on a screen (Hussars, Cuirassiers, Light Artillery, Grenadiers) use derived values, and Sappers be left out?
decisions.context: Only Skirmishers ($200) and Artillery ($1,000) costs are confirmed on screenshots.
decisions.suggestion: Derived costs taken, no Sappers. Default in force; reversible.

decisions.title: Should battles use simple numbers (8 rounds, 70% hit, rout at 25 health) with defenders fully visible?
decisions.context: The 1997 combat formulas are unknown; simple numbers are testable and the battle screen replays them.
decisions.suggestion: Taken. Default in force; reversible.

decisions.title: Should a country have at most one army per province (no merge order)?
decisions.context: Named armies with merge and split add about 3 orders and screens.
decisions.suggestion: One army per province taken. Default in force; reversible.

decisions.title: When upkeep cannot be paid, should the newest regiments be disbanded?
decisions.context: v2 has no credit rule (gap A8).
decisions.suggestion: Taken. Default in force; reversible.

decisions.title: Should Join the Empire, rail and sea moves, generals and medals stay out of v2?
decisions.context: Each adds orders and screens; colonies come only by conquest meanwhile.
decisions.suggestion: Taken (later milestone). Default in force; reversible.

decisions.title: Should a grant to the other Great Power give it the money?
decisions.context: In M6 a grant takes the money from the giver and no country receives it; it only raises relations. The 1997 rule is not documented.
decisions.suggestion: Taken: nobody receives it (a pure relations cost). Default in force; reversible.

decisions.title: Should prices on the partners market move only with the Great Powers' own deals, with no pull back toward the start price?
decisions.context: Before the review fix round the minors' fixed demand (24 goods a turn) and offers counted as excess demand, so goods ran to the 250% ceiling (clothing $2,250 by turn 35) and raw to the 50% floor by turn 30 whatever the players did. Now (FR-243) a price moves with the units the Great Powers bought minus the units they sold, as on the v1 world market. Measured at turn 40, seeds 1 to 4: clothing $648 to $710 (v1 world: $642), timber $144 to $180 (both computers buy it), no price at a bound. A nation that keeps buying or selling one commodity can still push it to a bound in time.
decisions.suggestion: Taken: Great Powers' deals only (FR-243). Alternative: a pull of about 10% a turn back toward the start price, so a constant push settles near 1.4 times the start; say if you want it.

decisions.title: Should the v2 trade baseline count the minors per nation or for both nations together?
decisions.context: FR-196 said "deals with at least 2 minors" without saying whose. Since the review fix round the computer opens a consulate only with a minor it will use (FR-245): nation 1 deals with all 4 minors, nation 2 only with Arvelia (Arvelia favours it and covers its 4 holds). A per-nation minimum would make the computer pay $500 for consulates it does not use.
decisions.suggestion: Taken: both nations together, at least 2 minors; each nation at least 1 minor and at least 1 purchase (FR-247).

decisions.title: Should the computer buy raw materials from minors, and open a consulate only where it will trade?
decisions.context: FR-193 had the computer bid only for lumber and steel, which no minor sells, so it never bought in "partners" and paid $2,000 for four consulates it used once. FR-245: it bids for the timber, coal, iron ore and cotton its mills lack (capped at what its partner minors offer), and orders a consulate only when the minors that favour it do not cover its holds. Score at turn 40 against the same player without raw bids, both nations summed: +82, +94, +25 and -20 (seeds 1 to 4).
decisions.suggestion: Taken (FR-245). Reversible; FR-247 pins its numbers.

decisions.title: Should a "world" market keep the v1 shape, with no mode key?

decisions.context: The rules say a freight car bought now carries goods next turn. The code lets it carry this turn (FR-039), which feels more responsive but differs from the original.

decisions.context: The rules charge canned food, clothing and furniture for a migrant, no cash. M3 follows that.

decisions.suggestion: Settled 2026-11-09 (NR-018): keep the 4-hold limit.

decisions.suggestion: Settled 2026-11-09 (NR-018): one-turn orders; repeat button only if play feels tedious.

decisions.title: Where should recruited and trained workers appear?
decisions.context: v1 creates no civilians after the start; recruits and trained workers join the industry workforce, and there is no University. The start civilians stay on the capital tile (rules 03).
decisions.suggestion: Settled 2026-11-12 (NR-029): leave it until a University or another civilian-producing rule exists.

decisions.title: How should the computer nation score better?
decisions.context: The new scripted player lays a few rail lines and builds depots as asked (NR-022). It ships far more (268 vs 181 units at turn 15) but scores slightly lower (382 vs 390), because extra goods sit unsold: 4 cargo holds cap sales at 32 units and stock is not scored.
